metaDescription: Pellet smokers that list at or below $500, compared on cooking area, controller and sear ability, plus a charcoal bullet as the budget contrast.
expertTake: The Pit Boss 700 Carbon is the best smoker under $500 because 718 sq in and a pellet controller give you room and automation in one box. The Pit Boss 500 FB2 is the value pick for a family of four who also wants a sear lever. If you only want to try smoking, skip this tier and buy a charcoal bullet. Check the current listing price before you buy.
introParagraphs: This is the tier where pellet smokers become affordable. An auger, a fire pot and a controller take over the work that a charcoal bullet leaves to you, and that automation is what the extra budget mostly buys. That is why this guide leans toward pellet cookers and uses the charcoal bullet as a contrast.

The differences between models come down to grate area, controller finish and a few features like a flame broiler. Prices move, so the $500 cap here reflects listing prices when this guide was updated. Compare the current listing before buying, and favor the model that fits your usual cook rather than your biggest holiday meal.

products.name: Pit Boss 700 Carbon Series Wood Pellet Grill and Smoker, 718 sq in
products.description:
The 700 Carbon is the largest pellet smoker in this group at 718 sq in, and that matters because room is the thing most buyers outgrow first. It fits two pork butts and a couple of racks of ribs with space to spare, where a 450 sq in cooker fills up quickly.

An LCD digital controller runs the auger and holds a set point across 180 to 500 F, which covers low smoke, roasting and baking. The maker pitches the surface as enough for dozens of patties, which is a useful picture of how much grate it offers.

It does not list WiFi, so you will stand at the panel or use a separate wireless thermometer. As with any pellet cooker, keep the hopper dry and the fire pot clean. It is the top choice if you cook for more than four and want to stay under the cap. Give it a full ten minute preheat before the meat goes on, and plan for a bigger pellet bill on long cooks, since a body this size burns more fuel. Put thick cuts at the center and leave room around each piece so smoke can circulate.
products.bestFor: Families that want the most grate for the money.
pros: 718 sq in is the largest area here
180 to 500 F range covers all recipes
LCD controller is easy to read

products.name: Pit Boss 500 FB2 Wood Pellet Grill and Smoker, 518 sq in
products.description:
The 500 FB2 spends its budget on a feature the others here lack: a flame broiler lever that exposes direct flame for searing up to 1,000 F. That turns a smoker into a grill that can finish steaks, which is rare in a pellet cooker at this price.

Its 518 sq in is enough for a household of four, and the LCD controller moves in 5 F increments across 180 to 500 F. That finer step gives better tuning than a dial, even if it is not PID.

It has less grate than the 700 Carbon, so choose it if the sear matters more than space. Keep the pellets dry and the fire pot clean, and cover the cooker between uses. A good habit is to practice with a thick steak before guests arrive, because the lever takes a few tries to master. Use the broiler only for the last minutes of a cook so you do not scorch the outside.
products.bestFor: Cooks who want to smoke and sear on the same machine.
pros: Flame broiler lever sears up to 1,000 F
518 sq in suits a family of four

products.name: Pit Boss 500 Carbon Series Wood Pellet Grill and Smoker, 543 sq in
products.description:
The 500 Carbon offers 543 sq in of cooking surface, a little more than the 500 FB2, with the same 180 to 500 F range and an LCD digital controller. It belongs to the newer Carbon series, which pairs a fresh body with the standard pellet recipe.

For most households the difference from the 500 FB2 is small. You gain about 25 sq in of grate and lose the flame broiler as a listed feature, so the choice depends on whether you want searing or a slightly bigger grate.

It is a straightforward pellet cooker with the usual care needs. Store pellets dry, vacuum the fire pot every few cooks and keep it covered. If you cook for a household that never sears, this is the slightly roomier of the two 500 models and the better buy. Compare the current listings, since the price gap between the two can swing either way.
products.bestFor: Buyers who want a mid-size pellet cooker without extras.
pros: 543 sq in is slightly bigger than the 500 FB2
LCD controller is simple to read

products.name: VEVOR 8-in-1 Wood Pellet Grill Smoker, 456 sq in
products.description:
The VEVOR is an 8-in-1 pellet cooker with a digital control panel, 456 sq in of cooking area and a dual-layer grilling space. Heavy-duty carbon steel makes up the body.

A dual-layer layout stacks two grates, which helps you cook different foods at different heights. That is useful for a family that wants ribs below and vegetables above, though the upper rack runs hotter.

It is a lesser-known brand than the Pit Boss models, so parts and support are a question to check. If you value a pellet unit at a low price and are comfortable with that risk, it is an option. Keep pellets dry and clean the pot. Keep a close eye on the first few cooks, since a newer controller may need calibrating against a separate thermometer. Check the manual for how the dual-layer grates are meant to be loaded so you do not block airflow.
products.bestFor: Budget buyers who want a pellet cooker with two grate levels.

products.name: Joyagrill 16-inch Multi-Layer Charcoal Smoker with Two Access Doors

specList.label: Fuel
specList.value: Charcoal and wood chips or dust

products.description:
This Joyagrill is the cheapest unit in the guide and a different kind of cooker. It is a 16-inch charcoal bullet with two cooking layers, two bigger access doors, a built-in thermometer and an air vent.

It shows what the extra budget buys: the pellet cookers add an auger and a controller, while this charcoal unit leaves fire and airflow to you. It makes real smoke flavor but needs attention every half hour and offers less capacity.

Choose it if you want to learn the craft or need a second smoker for camping. It also doubles as a fire pit and a grill. Keep it dry and cover it between uses. Start with a small load of charcoal and a few wood chunks, and keep the vents mostly open at first so the fire builds clean. A water pan, if you can fit one, steadies the temperature.
products.bestFor: Cooks who want the cheapest way to smoke or a second unit.
pros: Two access doors for adding fuel
Works as a smoker, grill or fire pit

buyingCriteria.explanation: Under $500 you get a pellet smoker with an auger and controller, where cheaper tiers give you charcoal or a simple element. The extra budget pays for automation and room. A 718 sq in grate on the 700 Carbon and 518 sq in on the 500 FB2 show how much grate this tier offers. Remember that pellet use adds to the real running cost, so a smaller grate can save money over a year.

buyingCriteria.criterion: Choose grate area for your household
buyingCriteria.explanation: A household of four needs roughly 400 to 500 sq in, which is where the VEVOR at 456 sq in, the 500 FB2 at 518 sq in and the 500 Carbon at 543 sq in sit. The 700 Carbon at 718 sq in suits larger families. A bigger body burns more pellets and takes longer to heat. Measure your largest cut before you buy, since a packer brisket needs more width than most cookers here offer.

The 500 FB2 lists a flame broiler lever that reaches 1,000 F on direct flame. Most pellet cookers top out at 450 to 500 F, so a broiler gives you a real sear. If you cook steaks, it is worth choosing over a bigger grate. Searing on a pellet cooker still lags a charcoal grill, so set expectations accordingly.

The Pit Boss models use LCD controllers with steps like 5 F, while the VEVOR uses a digital controller. None here list PID or WiFi, so keep a separate probe and check the temperature against the display on your first cook. Calibrate by checking the display against a probe on your first run, since no listing here promises PID control.

Pit Boss parts are widely available, while the VEVOR has less track record. Pellet cookers need igniters, augers and probes over time, so parts support matters in year three. Ask about warranty terms on the controller, igniter and auger before you buy.

Pellet smokers need an outlet and dry pellets. Store pellets in a sealed bin, and keep the cooker covered. Pellet costs add up over a year, so factor them in. A cover and a dry pellet bin cost little and protect the whole investment.

Prices move, so read these as relative tiers rather than fixed numbers.

cards.label: Pellet
cards.text: The Pit Boss and VEVOR cookers run on an auger and controller. They hold a set point and need less attention, but cost more and need power. A pellet unit also holds temperature through a windy night far better than a bullet.

cards.label: Charcoal
cards.text: The Joyagrill is cheap and makes real smoke, but you tend the fire and it holds less. It makes strong smoke but asks for a check every half hour.

howToChoose.note: Pick pellet for automation, charcoal to save money and learn. A charcoal bullet also costs less to replace if you decide smoking is not for you.

howToChoose.intro: Searing and space pull in opposite directions at this budget, so decide which matters more.

howToChoose.subheading: For Weekend Brisket and Ribs Specifically

cards.label: Look for
cards.text: Enough grate to fit the meat flat, a controller that holds a set point and a hopper that lasts through the cook. A probe in the meat is more reliable than timing alone.

cards.label: In this comparison
cards.text: The 700 Carbon at 718 sq in is the best fit, with the 500 Carbon at 543 sq in as a smaller option. With 718 sq in you can also cook sides at the same time, which saves a second oven or grill.

cards.label: Spend more if
cards.text: You want WiFi, PID control or a heavier body. The next tier adds those. Those features also tend to come with sturdier bodies and better parts support.

cards.label: Save if
cards.text: You want to try smoking. The Joyagrill is the cheapest start. Put the savings into a probe thermometer and a cover.

maintenance.why: Ash chokes airflow and causes flameouts. Check the igniter hole is clear. A narrow-nozzle shop vacuum reaches the igniter hole without scattering ash across the grate.
Grease can ignite at high heat. Replace liners regularly. Wipe the drip tray and the bucket beneath it too, since fat collects in corners and feeds fires.
Damp pellets swell and jam the auger. Use a sealed bin. A sealed metal bin with a gasket lid works better than the original bag, which wicks moisture from a damp garage.
A greasy probe misreads temperature. Wipe gently. Test it against boiling water as a quick check, since a probe that reads far off will confuse the controller.
Rain damages electronics and rusts steel. A vented cover avoids trapped condensation that a fully sealed one can cause in humid weather.

faq.q: Is a pellet smoker under $500 good?
faq.a: Yes. It automates feed and temperature, which makes smoking easier. The smoke is milder than charcoal, but the results are consistent. Cooks who smoke monthly will notice the difference most in how little attention a pellet unit needs.
The Pit Boss 700 Carbon at 718 sq in. The 500 Carbon at 543 sq in and the 500 FB2 at 518 sq in follow. Grate area also affects pellet use, so a smaller unit is cheaper to run on weeknights.
The 500 FB2 has a flame broiler that reaches 1,000 F. The others top out near 500 F. Use the lever only for the last few minutes to avoid scorching the outside.
